sections.title: Part 1 · Listening to Problem Solving
sections.instructions: Listen to the conversation and answer the questions.
sections.passage:
MANAGER: SecureSpace Storage, this is Devon.
CUSTOMER: Hi Devon, it's Farah Nasser, unit 214. I came in today and found a water stain across the ceiling and two of my boxes are damp.
MANAGER: I'm sorry to hear that, Farah. We had a roof leak reported in that wing last Thursday after the storm. Do you remember what was in the damp boxes?
CUSTOMER: Mostly winter clothing, but one box had photo albums.
MANAGER: I understand photos can't really be replaced. Our facility policy covers damage up to five hundred dollars per unit, but you'd need to have signed up for the optional contents insurance, which is eight dollars a month.
CUSTOMER: I don't think I did. I just took the basic unit rental.
MANAGER: Let me check... you're right, you have the basic plan, so the facility isn't able to cover the contents. What I can offer is a free unit transfer to a dry section on the second floor, and I'll waive next month's rent as an apology.
CUSTOMER: That doesn't help the photos that are already damaged. Is there anything you can do about that?
MANAGER: I can have our restoration partner assess the albums at no charge; sometimes photos can be dried and saved if it's caught early enough. I'll need you to bring them to the front desk within 48 hours for the best chance.
CUSTOMER: I can bring them tomorrow morning. What about the clothing?
MANAGER: Since clothing isn't usually salvageable once mildew sets in, I can't offer a repair, but I'll extend the waived rent to two months instead of one, given the loss.
CUSTOMER: All right, I'll take the transfer and bring the albums in tomorrow.
MANAGER: I'll have the new unit ready by two o'clock, and I'll email you the transfer confirmation.

sections.title: Part 4 · Listening to a News Item

sections.passage: ANNOUNCER: The Eastview Public Library system announced today that it is permanently eliminating late fines on all items, effective the first of next month. Officials say fines rarely recovered lost materials and instead discouraged low-income families, who accounted for a disproportionate share of blocked accounts. Under the old system, unpaid fines over fifteen dollars froze a patron's borrowing privileges, and internal data showed nearly forty thousand cardholders were currently blocked. Items that are significantly overdue, more than sixty days, will still be marked lost and billed at replacement cost, but that charge is waived if the item is returned in usable condition. The library expects to lose about two hundred thousand dollars a year in fine revenue, but says this is offset by reduced staff time spent processing small payments. Similar policies have already been adopted in several major cities, with early data suggesting a modest increase in the return of overdue materials once the fear of penalty was removed. The city council approved the change unanimously.

sections.title: Part 6 · Listening for Viewpoints
sections.instructions: Listen to the two speakers and answer the questions.
sections.passage:
SPEAKER A: Personalized news feeds get an unfair amount of blame. They surface stories people actually want to read, which keeps them engaged with current events at all, rather than avoiding the news entirely because it feels overwhelming. Engagement itself isn't the enemy.
SPEAKER B: The problem isn't engagement, it's what gets amplified to achieve it. Outrage and emotionally charged stories spread fastest, so the algorithm doesn't just reflect our interests, it shapes them, often toward the most divisive framing of any given issue.
SPEAKER A: That's a real risk, but plenty of platforms have adjusted their ranking to downweight outrage bait, and users can also follow specific outlets directly to bypass the algorithm altogether.
SPEAKER B: Few users actually do that, though. Most people accept the default feed, and defaults have enormous power over behaviour. I'd also point out that a feed optimized for individual preference fragments the shared set of facts a society needs to debate policy together.
SPEAKER A: I agree that shared facts matter, but the alternative, a single centrally chosen news feed for everyone, raises its own problems about who gets to decide what's important.
SPEAKER B: True, which is why I favour transparency requirements over either extreme: platforms should have to disclose how a feed is ranked, so users can at least understand what they're seeing and why.

options: Outrage content should be promoted more

Algorithms should be banned from social media
Personalized feeds keep people engaged with the news rather than avoiding it
questions.explanation: Speaker A says personalized feeds keep people engaged rather than avoiding the news.

From: Owen Fairweather <owen@fairweatherlandscaping.ca>
To: Naomi Whitfield <n.whitfield@rosehill-condos.ca>
Subject: Invoice #2291 — Spring Cleanup

Dear Ms. Whitfield,

Please find attached invoice #2291 for the spring cleanup at Rosehill Condos, totaling $3,840. This includes $2,100 for the agreed scope, which was bed edging, mulching, and hedge trimming across all common areas, plus $1,740 for removal of a fallen tree limb on April 9, which was not part of our original contract.

We treated the limb removal as urgent, since it was blocking the east parking entrance, and completed it the same day we discovered it, without waiting for approval given the safety concern.

Payment is due within 15 days of the invoice date, which is May 2.

Regards,
Owen Fairweather

------------------------------

From: Naomi Whitfield <n.whitfield@rosehill-condos.ca>
To: Owen Fairweather
Subject: Re: Invoice #2291 — Spring Cleanup

Dear Mr. Fairweather,

Thank you for the invoice. The $2,100 for the contracted work is approved and will be paid on time.

However, I cannot approve the $1,740 limb removal charge without board authorization, since our contract requires written approval for any work exceeding $500 outside the agreed scope, regardless of urgency. I understand the safety concern, and I don't dispute that the work was necessary, but the approval requirement exists precisely for situations like this, to prevent disputes over cost.

I will bring this to the board at our meeting on May 8, and I expect a decision by May 10. In the meantime, could you send an itemized breakdown of the $1,740, including hours worked and equipment used? That will help the board evaluate the charge fairly.

I would also like to note that had we been contacted before the work began, we might have arranged for a lower-cost provider already on-site that day for an unrelated job. I raise this not to assign blame, but so the board understands why they may ask questions about the amount.

Regards,
Naomi Whitfield

sections.title: Reading Part 3 · Reading for Information
sections.instructions: Read the article and answer the questions.
sections.passageTitle: The hidden cost of food waste
sections.passage:
Roughly a third of all food produced worldwide is never eaten, a figure that surprises most people once they hear it, because waste is rarely visible in a single household. It happens instead in small amounts across an enormous system: unharvested crops left in fields because of a market price drop, produce rejected by grocery stores for cosmetic blemishes, and meals scraped into the bin at home.

The environmental cost is larger than most people assume. Producing food that is never eaten consumes water, land, and fuel for nothing, and rotting food in landfills releases methane, a greenhouse gas many times more potent than carbon dioxide over a short time horizon. Some researchers estimate that if food waste were a country, it would rank third in greenhouse gas emissions, behind only the United States and China.

Solutions have emerged at every stage of the supply chain. Some retailers now sell "ugly" produce at a discount rather than discarding it, and a handful of apps connect restaurants with unsold meals to nearby customers at the end of the day. On farms, better weather forecasting and storage technology have reduced losses from spoilage before crops even reach a truck.

Yet household waste remains the largest single category in wealthy countries, accounting for nearly half of all food wasted, ahead of retail and food service combined. Researchers attribute this partly to confusing date labels: many consumers cannot distinguish a "best before" date, which refers to quality, from a "use by" date, which refers to safety, and so discard food that is still perfectly edible.

Some governments have begun standardizing labels to address this confusion, and early results from regions that simplified their labelling systems suggest a measurable decline in household waste, though researchers caution that changing labels alone has not eliminated the problem, since habits and a lack of planning around grocery shopping remain significant contributing factors.

questions.label: Question 1
questions.question: What is the main idea of the article?
options: Food waste has a large environmental cost and requires solutions at multiple stages, including in households
Only farmers are responsible for food waste
Food waste has recently become a problem for the first time
Grocery stores are the largest source of food waste
questions.explanation: The article covers causes across the supply chain and emphasizes household waste.

questions.label: Question 2
questions.question: Why is food waste hard to notice?
options: It is deliberately hidden by food companies
It happens in small amounts spread across a large system
It happens only during specific seasons
It occurs mostly outside urban areas
questions.explanation: The article says waste occurs in small amounts across an enormous system.

questions.label: Question 3
questions.question: Why is rotting food environmentally harmful?
options: It contaminates groundwater directly
It releases methane, a potent greenhouse gas
It increases landfill fees for cities
It attracts pests to landfills
questions.explanation: Rotting food releases methane, described as far more potent than carbon dioxide short-term.

questions.label: Question 4
questions.question: According to some researchers, where would food waste rank among countries by emissions?
options: Third, behind the United States and China
It would not rank among the top emitters
Tenth
First, ahead of all countries
questions.explanation: The article cites an estimate ranking food waste third.

questions.label: Question 5
questions.question: What example is given of a retail-level solution?
options: Selling "ugly" produce at a discount
Increasing the price of fresh produce
Reducing store hours
Banning the sale of processed foods
questions.explanation: Retailers sell cosmetically rejected produce at a discount rather than discarding it.

questions.label: Question 6
questions.question: What is the largest single category of food waste in wealthy countries?
options: Retail waste
Household waste
Food service waste
Farm-level waste
questions.explanation: Household waste accounts for nearly half of all food wasted, more than retail and food service combined.

questions.label: Question 7
questions.question: Why do many consumers throw away food that is still edible?
options: They lack refrigeration space
They distrust food that looks imperfect
They are following government guidelines
They confuse "best before" and "use by" date labels
questions.explanation: The confusion between quality and safety labels leads to unnecessary disposal.

questions.label: Question 8
questions.question: What has happened in regions that simplified food labels?
options: Retail waste increased instead
A measurable decline in household waste, though the problem was not eliminated
No measurable change occurred
Household waste disappeared entirely
questions.explanation: Simplified labelling led to a decline, but researchers say habits and planning remain factors.

questions.label: Question 9
questions.question: What do researchers say is still a challenge even after label reform?
options: A lack of government funding
Farmers' resistance to new technology
The cost of new labels
Habits and a lack of planning around grocery shopping
questions.explanation: The article notes these as significant contributing factors that remain despite label changes.

sections.title: Reading Part 4 · Reading for Viewpoints
sections.instructions: Read the two viewpoints and answer the questions.
sections.passage:
Invest in Free Tuition
By Selena Vance

Charging tuition treats education as a private purchase rather than a public good, and the consequences are visible in the data. Students from low-income families graduate with far more debt on average, and that debt shapes decisions for decades, from delaying home ownership to avoiding lower-paid but socially valuable careers such as teaching or social work. Countries that have made university free, funded through general taxation, have not seen quality collapse; several rank among the highest in the world for research output. Free tuition would not eliminate every barrier a student faces, but it would remove the single largest one for most families.

Free Isn't Fair
By Tobias Reyes

"Free" tuition is never actually free; it simply shifts the cost from students who benefit directly to taxpayers, many of whom never attend university and will earn less over their lifetimes than graduates typically do. That amounts to a transfer from lower earners to future higher earners. A better approach targets aid at those who need it most, through income-based grants and loan repayment tied to post-graduation earnings, so someone who struggles financially after graduating pays little, while someone who becomes a surgeon repays proportionally more. Universal free tuition, by contrast, spends the same public money on the wealthiest students as on the neediest.

questions.label: Question 1
questions.question: What is the main topic of the two pieces?
options: Whether online degrees are as valuable as in-person ones
How governments should fund research
How to reduce classroom sizes
Whether university tuition should be free for all students
questions.explanation: Both authors debate free versus paid university tuition.

questions.label: Question 2
questions.question: What does Vance say about students from low-income families?
options: They graduate with more debt, which affects major life decisions
They are less likely to attend university at all
They prefer vocational training over university
They receive more financial aid than other students
questions.explanation: She says their debt shapes decisions like home ownership and career choice.

questions.label: Question 3
questions.question: What does Vance say about countries with free tuition?
options: Quality has declined significantly
They have reduced the number of universities
They have eliminated all barriers to education
Quality has not collapsed, and several rank highly for research
questions.explanation: She says several such countries rank among the highest for research output.

questions.label: Question 4
questions.question: What is Reyes's central argument against free tuition?
options: It shifts costs to taxpayers who will often earn less than graduates, favouring future high earners
Free tuition would bankrupt governments immediately
Free tuition would reduce the number of applicants
Free tuition is illegal in most countries
questions.explanation: He argues it transfers cost from students to taxpayers, many of whom earn less over their lifetimes.

questions.label: Question 5
questions.question: What alternative does Reyes propose?
options: Income-based grants and loan repayment tied to post-graduation earnings
Charging all students the same fixed tuition
Eliminating public funding for universities entirely
Requiring employers to pay tuition directly
questions.explanation: He proposes aid and repayment tied to income after graduation.

questions.label: Question 6
questions.question: According to Reyes, what is a flaw in universal free tuition?
options: It requires students to work part-time
It spends the same public money on wealthy students as on needy ones
It reduces the quality of teaching
It cannot be implemented at large universities
questions.explanation: He says universal free tuition doesn't distinguish between wealthy and needy students.

questions.label: Question 7
questions.question: What does Vance acknowledge as a limitation of her proposal?
options: Free tuition would reduce research funding
Free tuition would take decades to implement
Free tuition would not eliminate every barrier students face
Free tuition would only help wealthy students
questions.explanation: She admits it would not remove every barrier, just the largest one.

questions.label: Question 8
questions.question: How does Reyes characterize the effect of free tuition on taxpayers?
options: A benefit to all taxpayers equally
A transfer from lower earners to future higher earners
A cost that only affects wealthy taxpayers
A neutral effect with no real winners or losers
questions.explanation: He describes free tuition funded by general taxation as such a transfer.

questions.label: Question 9
questions.question: What underlying value does Vance's argument rest on?
options: Education is a public good that society should invest in collectively
Individual achievement should determine access to education
Universities should compete for private funding
Taxes should be lowered across the board
questions.explanation: Her opening statement frames tuition as treating education as a public good versus a private purchase.

questions.label: Question 10
questions.question: What underlying value does Reyes's argument rest on?
options: Public spending should be targeted based on need and ability to repay
Government funding for universities should end
Wealthy students should pay more in all circumstances
Education should be entirely privatized
questions.explanation: His proposal for income-based aid reflects a focus on targeting resources by need.

sections.title: Writing Task 1 · Email
sections.instructions: Write an email based on the task below.

writingTask.title: Writing an Email
writingTask.scenario: You are the treasurer of a small community club. A vendor overcharged the club by $180 on a recent invoice for event supplies, and the mistake was only noticed after payment was made. Write an email to the vendor.
instructions: Explain which invoice you are referring to and what the error was.
Describe how you discovered the mistake.
Request a specific resolution and a deadline.
Keep a polite but firm tone.
writingTask.sampleAnswer: Dear Mr. Petrov, I am writing regarding invoice #5567 for supplies delivered to our club event on September 6, which we paid in full on September 10. While reconciling our accounts this week, our bookkeeper noticed that we were charged for 60 folding chairs at $8 each, but our order form and your own delivery slip both confirm only 38 chairs were delivered. This comes to an overcharge of $176, plus a $4 discrepancy in the delivery fee, for a total of $180. I have attached both the original order form and the delivery slip for your reference. As our club operates on a limited budget raised entirely through memberships, I would appreciate a refund of $180 to the account originally charged, or a credit toward our next order if that is easier for your records. Could you confirm which option is possible by the end of next week? I have valued working with your company on past events and hope we can resolve this quickly. Thank you for your attention to this matter. Sincerely, Corinne Beaulieu, Treasurer

sections.title: Writing Task 2 · Survey Response
sections.instructions: Write a response to the survey questions below.

writingTask.title: Responding to Survey Questions
writingTask.scenario: Your workplace is deciding whether to replace its annual in-person holiday party with an extra paid day off, or to keep the party but make it optional rather than mandatory attendance. Complete the survey explaining which option you prefer and why.
instructions: Give at least two reasons for your choice, using specific examples.
Address one possible concern about your choice and respond to it.
writingTask.sampleAnswer: I would prefer keeping the party but making attendance optional. First, many employees genuinely enjoy the event and look forward to it as a chance to connect with colleagues outside of regular meetings, so removing it entirely would take away something meaningful for those people. Second, making attendance optional respects employees who have family obligations, religious observances, or simply prefer not to attend evening events, without forcing them to give up something they value in exchange for a day off they may not want either. Some might worry that optional attendance would make the party feel poorly attended or awkward for organizers planning catering numbers. This is a fair concern, but it could be addressed by asking employees to RSVP two weeks in advance, which would let organizers plan realistic numbers and avoid waste. I believe this approach balances flexibility with keeping a valued tradition alive, and it avoids replacing one rigid policy with another. Thank you for asking for employee input on this decision.

sections.title: Speaking Task 1 · Giving Advice
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 1: Giving Advice
speakingTask.scenario: A friend has been offered a promotion that pays more but requires relocating to a city far from their family, and they are torn about what to do. Give your friend advice on how to think through the decision.
tips: Acknowledge that this is a hard decision.
Give two or three specific factors to consider.
Avoid simply telling them what to choose; help them think it through.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: This sounds like a genuinely difficult decision, and there's no single right answer. I would suggest starting by listing what matters most to you long-term, not just right now, since career and family both matter at different points in life. It might help to ask whether the relocation is permanent or could be revisited in a year or two if it doesn't work out. I'd also suggest talking honestly with your family about how often you could visit, and whether technology could keep you closely connected. Finally, consider whether a similar opportunity might come up again if you turn this one down, since that can lower the pressure to decide perfectly right now.

sections.title: Speaking Task 2 · Talking about a Personal Experience
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 2: Talking about a Personal Experience
speakingTask.scenario: Describe a time when you received feedback that was hard to hear but ultimately helped you improve. Explain what happened and how you responded.
tips: Set the scene briefly.
Describe your initial reaction honestly.
Explain how you used the feedback afterward.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: A few years ago, my supervisor told me that my reports were accurate but too long, and that people were skimming rather than reading them carefully. At first I felt defensive, since I had put a lot of effort into being thorough. But after thinking about it, I realized her point was fair. I started using clear headings and a short summary at the top of each report. Within a few months, colleagues told me my reports were much easier to use, and I felt genuinely proud of the improvement.

sections.title: Speaking Task 3 · Describing a Scene
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 3: Describing a Scene
speakingTask.scenario: Describe a small neighbourhood bakery early in the morning, just as it opens. Include what you see, smell, and hear, and what the baker and early customers are doing.
tips: Use vivid sensory details.
Move through the scene in a logical order.
Include at least two specific actions by people in the scene.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: The bakery is warm and dimly lit compared to the grey morning outside, and the smell of fresh bread and cinnamon fills the air the moment the door opens. Behind the counter, the baker pulls a tray of golden croissants from the oven, humming quietly to herself. A line has already formed, with two regulars chatting near the register while a young man checks his watch, clearly on his way to work. The soft clink of the cash register and the crinkle of paper bags add to the cozy, unhurried rhythm of the morning.

sections.title: Speaking Task 4 · Making Predictions
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 4: Making Predictions
speakingTask.scenario: A teenager stands nervously outside a closed office door holding a folder of documents, glancing repeatedly at a clock on the wall. Predict what will happen next and explain your reasoning.
tips: Base predictions on specific details in the scene.
Use prediction language such as will probably and is likely to.
Give a clear sequence of events.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: Given the folder of documents and the nervous glances at the clock, I think the teenager is probably waiting for an important appointment, perhaps a job interview or a meeting about school admission. When the door opens, they will likely take a deep breath before walking in, trying to appear calm despite their nerves. During the meeting, they will probably answer questions carefully, referring to their documents when needed. Afterward, I imagine they will feel a mix of relief and uncertainty, replaying the conversation in their mind as they wait to hear the outcome.

sections.title: Speaking Task 5 · Comparing and Persuading
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 5: Comparing and Persuading
speakingTask.scenario: Your book club must choose a format for meetings. Option A is meeting in person once a month at a local café, which costs each member about $8 for coffee but limits attendance to people who live nearby. Option B is meeting online every two weeks for free, which anyone can join but which several members feel is less personal. Persuade the group to choose one option.
tips: State your preferred option clearly.
Compare both options directly using details from the scenario.
Address the main weakness of your choice.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: I recommend keeping the in-person café meetings. Although it costs a little money and excludes members who live farther away, meeting face-to-face builds a stronger sense of community and makes discussions feel warmer and more natural, which several of us have said we miss with video calls. The eight-dollar cost is minor compared to what we already spend on books each month. For members who cannot attend regularly, we could send discussion notes afterward so they don't feel excluded. Overall, the personal connection is worth far more than the convenience of meeting online.

sections.title: Speaking Task 6 · Dealing with a Difficult Situation
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 6: Dealing with a Difficult Situation
speakingTask.scenario: You booked a non-refundable vacation rental for a family trip, but two days before departure, the host cancels citing a plumbing emergency and offers only a partial refund. Explain what you would say to the host and what steps you would take next.
tips: Stay calm and businesslike.
Explain what you would say to the host directly.
Describe your backup plan if the situation isn't resolved.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: I would first ask the host to clarify the platform's cancellation policy, since a host-initiated cancellation this close to arrival often entitles guests to a full refund, not just a partial one. I would say, "I understand emergencies happen, but since this cancellation wasn't caused by me, I'd like a full refund as outlined in the platform's policy." If the host refused, I would contact the platform's support team directly and provide our booking confirmation as evidence. At the same time, I would start searching for alternative accommodations immediately, since we only have two days, rather than waiting for the dispute to be resolved first.

sections.title: Speaking Task 7 · Expressing Opinions
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 7: Expressing Opinions
speakingTask.scenario: Some people believe social media companies should be legally required to verify the age of every user. Do you agree or disagree? Support your opinion with reasons.
tips: State a clear opinion at the start.
Give two or three supported reasons.
Acknowledge a counterargument and respond to it.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: I agree that age verification should be required, though I recognize it raises real challenges. First, it would help protect children from content and interactions that are not appropriate for their age, which is an important child-safety goal. Second, it could reduce the pressure young people feel from features designed for adult attention spans, such as endless scrolling. Some argue that verification threatens privacy, since it may require submitting identification, and that is a legitimate worry. However, this could be addressed by using privacy-protecting verification methods, such as third-party services that confirm age without storing personal documents. On balance, I believe the benefit to child safety outweighs the risk, provided privacy safeguards are built in carefully.

sections.title: Speaking Task 8 · Describing an Unusual Situation
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 8: Describing an Unusual Situation
speakingTask.scenario: You see a photo of a small floating village where houses are built on rafts connected by wooden walkways, with boats used instead of cars. Describe it to a friend and explain whether you would like to visit or live there.
tips: Describe the most distinctive features first.
Imagine daily life for the people who live there.
Give a clear personal opinion with reasons.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: This village is unlike anywhere I've seen. Wooden houses float on rafts, connected by narrow walkways that sway slightly with the water, and instead of cars, small boats are tied up outside each home like bicycles. Daily life there must move at a different pace, with fishing and boat travel woven into ordinary routines like going to school or visiting a neighbour. I would love to visit for a few days, since it seems peaceful and completely different from city life, though I think living there permanently would take some getting used to, especially during storms.
